entries.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (Pando)
entries.by: Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau and Ted Nyman, OpenAI
entries.summary: Agent fan-out broke stock Git hosting. Dropping repo-wide ref snapshots (moving to causal consistency) and dropping per-client packs (reusing cached packs via packfile-uri) cut median push latency about 80% at about 1 PB/day.

entries.title: The 5 layers of agent memory
entries.summary: Working, episodic, semantic, procedural and meta-memory. Each layer fails the same way: the store exists, but the read, dedupe, reflection or garbage-collection step that keeps it useful is missing.

entries.title: The best Claude setup is no setup
entries.summary: Config written for older models rots, so wipe instructions, skills and memory, default to Auto, prompt with Goal + Context, and ask for HTML pages instead of .docx. Sound principle (prune and re-baseline after model upgrades), weak procedure: no before/after eval, and it deletes project facts and rationale along with obsolete capability patches.

entries.title: Second Brain OS: the five-layer map of AI agents
entries.summary: An agent is the model plus five layers, each answering one question: context (what it sees), loop (who decides), gate (who sorts), harness (what it can reach), evals (how you know). A failure in one layer looks like another, so name the layer before blaming the model.

entries.title: 6 must-know terms for AI agent harnesses
entries.summary: Agent = model + harness; six concepts: agent loop, tool calling, context management, checkpointing, permissions and sandboxing, guardrails. Good vocabulary, shallow treatment. The comments add what's missing: observability and trajectory evals, and the point that checkpoint-and-resume is only safe when write tools are idempotent.

entries.title: PageIndex: reasoning-based retrieval for long documents
entries.summary: Replaces chunk-and-embed RAG with a per-document section tree. An agent reads the tree, then fetches tight page ranges and cites pages. In the repo's own 10-K notebook it scored 100% at about $110 per 1,000 queries; the best vector run was 92% at $134. Wins on long, structured documents; costs several strong-model turns per query and depends on a correct outline.

entries.title: AI crash projects for public good: Mollick's post and the evidence behind it
entries.summary: Mollick wants national crash projects in tutoring, health second opinions, financial literacy and government services using current models. The evidence says the bottleneck is the harness (steering toward augmentation, eliciting context, cheap oversight), not the model: students who let AI write kept nothing, and the medical agent was safe only with a physician watching live.

entries.title: MIT Technology Review's Intro to AI mini-course
entries.summary: A six-part beginner course: definitions, a hands-on chatbot exercise, how to talk about AI (including with kids), traps (bias, hallucination, unreliable detection, deepfakes), work and regulation. Durable on judgment (iterate and correct, a fit-for-purpose rule, verify, don't anthropomorphize); dated on tools (no agents or reasoning models) and US policy. The summary adds a checklist for an updated curriculum.

entries.title: Psychology of programming and deterministic workflows
entries.summary: Framing matters more than programming: "agent" is a naming convention, and teams write hundreds of lines to steer one. Design the workflow instead, route with CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md to Markdown step files, and use the model as the runtime. Sound reframe, but a model reading Markdown is not deterministic: that has to come from a fixed route, scripts, failing checks and placed human gates.

entries.title: Do humans still need to check AI's facts? (Mollick on BrowseComp and DeepFact)
entries.by: Ethan Mollick, plus BrowseComp and DeepFact
entries.summary: Mollick says human fact-checking of AI is an outdated default. The numbers hold, but BrowseComp tests finding, not checking, and DeepFact's error-heavy test set lets a constant answer score 83.9%. DeepFact's best result is humans auditing agent evidence (90.9%): redesign the human as an auditor of routed disagreements, measure reviewers with planted canaries, and version eval labels.

entries.title: Elephant-Goldfish Model: deep-context drafting, zero-context review
entries.by: Shubham Saboo, Google's EGM plugin and Dave Rensin's essay
entries.summary: The agent that drafts a spec (Elephant, full conversation) should not review it; reviewers (Goldfish) are fresh subagents that see only the doc and the files it links, so unstated assumptions surface. Sound idea, heavy plugin: fresh context removes conversational bias but not shared model priors, isolation leaks on some hosts, write boundaries are convention only, and Rensin's own hit rate is about 30% of critic findings, with no eval.

entries.title: Ruben Hassid's six levels of Claude, checked
entries.summary: A consumer setup guide in six levels. Two claims hold against Anthropic's own pages: thumbs feedback stores the whole conversation for up to 5 years and may train models, and an owner turning org memory off permanently deletes every member's memory. Switching models mid-chat costs a cold cache, not a "re-read". Takeaways: pin model and effort per conversation, write a feedback-button policy, put the org memory toggle under change control, version config instead of wiping it.

entries.title: s3: agent swarms that learn their own coordination
entries.by: Elvis Saravia (DAIR.AI) on Jha et al.
entries.summary: N copies of one small model, no roles or orchestrator, just message/read tools in an async harness, trained with GRPO on one max-over-team reward. Learns broadcast-once for pooling private facts (93% vs 35% for online SFT at N=4) and branch-claiming for search. Per-agent reward breeds a public-goods dilemma where agents go silent. Caveats: toy tasks, 0.6B/1.7B models, no win over best-of-4 at training size after correction.

entries.title: The model proposes, the harness enforces
entries.summary: LLM conclusions are non-monotonic: reordering, reframing or a long context can overturn an answer nothing contradicted, and the model keeps no ledger of which conclusion rests on which fact, unlike designed belief-revision systems. So guarantees must come from the deterministic harness, defined as whatever you would still trust if the model were trying to fool you. Applied to tests: the runner and property- or reference-checked generated inputs are harness; assertions written by the implementing agent are not ("a mirror with a green light on it"); spec-derived tests need human sign-off; mutation testing checks a test can fail. Cites a reported Codex CLI incident (#59060) where a reboot request wrecked a server. Essay, not study: the ordering experiment is anecdotal, "non-monotonic" is used loosely, and a second agent on the same model and spec adds less independence than it seems.

entries.title: DeepSeek's Super-agent: one router, a ticket per task
entries.summary: One long-lived main Session listens to GitHub (and Feishu), a deterministic gate decides who may start work, the model assesses the rest against team-written rules, and each accepted Ticket gets an immutable Mandate (scope, strength, policy version) and its own Executor Session and directory. Later messages reach the Ticket by subscription as context only, with no new authority. Proactive work starts in `observe` mode (record "would accept", do nothing). The post's Watchdog for loops and drift is not in the code, only an hourly liveness check; its numbers (3 to 5 sessions per person, 16 vs 29 min on one task) are press reports of the article. The value is the authority model, not the router topology.

entries.title: Shivani Virdi's six-stage AI engineering reading list
entries.summary: 19 sources in six stages: LLM fundamentals, prompting in production (a prompt is code), context engineering, harness, evals, observability. Current (half from 2026) but Anthropic-heavy (12 of 19). Its strongest sources: Anthropic's planner/generator/evaluator harness (a skeptical evaluator driving the app via Playwright with hard thresholds and per-sprint contracts; $200 and 6 h vs $9 solo, and only the harness build worked; re-test and remove components on each model release), OpenAI's harness engineering (about 1M lines, no hand-written code; a 100-line AGENTS.md as a map over checked docs, mechanically enforced layers, per-worktree observability, garbage-collection agents) and the prompt-versioning cookbook (immutable server-side versions, pin in production, the pin is what gets reviewed). Missing: the loop from traces to failure analysis to evals to the next change, harness subtraction as a practice, prompt change control, and security.

entries.title: Building a coding agent from scratch: an open harness-engineering course
entries.by: Paul Iusztin on Decoding AI's course repo
entries.summary: Builds "decode", a Claude Code-style agent in Python on Pydantic AI: a ~20-line ReAct loop over nine tools, then the harness around it in eight lessons (sandbox in Docker or Modal, memory, skills, LSP, compaction at ~80%, Explore subagents and personas, headless remote runs by CLI/webhook/cron, a 19-task benchmark plus regression suite in Opik, Kitaru record-and-replay). Repo keeps ADRs, a glossary and milestone capstone tests. Caveats: sponsor tools (Modal, Opik, Kitaru) are baked in, the design drew on Claude Code's leaked source, the "harness beats model" headline is LangChain's Terminal-Bench result, and 19 tasks is too few to rank harness changes.

entries.title: InfraRSI: contract-locked agents for training-throughput tuning
entries.summary: A self-improving agent harness that speeds up distributed LLM training by searching launch settings and source patches together. The contribution is the verifier: before any edit, `init` locks a task contract (tokens per update, loss tolerance, allowed precisions) and hashes frozen files (data, loss, timers); `doctor` calibrates per-cluster timing noise; five invariant layers (execution, workload, schedule, numerical, timing) and back-to-back re-runs gate promotion, else the delivered speedup is 1.00×. Search keeps global time and censored peak-memory models over all trials (OOMs included) and a cross-hardware experience bank. Four dense and MoE workloads on 8 to 16 H100/H200: 1.83× geomean, mean MFU 17.4% to 30.0%, up to 2.75×; beats RE-Bench's scaffold (1.37×). Offline re-verification rejected 33% of 1,212 runs, and the LLM's own speedup predictions correlated negatively with measurements. Caveats: throughput only, some hacks caught only by human source review, four workloads, no replication.

entries.title: LongCapHarness: a written harness instead of long-context training
entries.by: Elvis Saravia (DAIR.AI) on Zhang and He, Microsoft Research Asia
entries.summary: A strong model (GPT-5.6-Sol) splits each long-context task type into capability primitives (code for rules like lookup, counting and ordering; bounded LLM calls for judgements), writes control logic and state that live outside the model's context, and refines them by recursive self-improvement on a dev set; the frozen harness library then runs a small model with an 8K or 32K window. HELMET plus RULER: Llama3-8B 15.14 to 79.32 (+64.18) with no training, above NExtLong-128K (70.15); transfers to Qwen2.5-3B (78.73 vs PolicyLong 64.10); about $541 in API tokens vs $1.9K to $3.7K of GPU time. Caveats: the dev split covers every evaluated task type, perfect Recall comes from code, ICL/RAG/LongQA barely move, small models cannot build their own harness, and inference input tokens roughly double.

entries.title: HybridAgent: agents that think in latent space and act in text
entries.by: Aishwarya Naresh Reganti on Zou et al.
entries.summary: Inside one generation the agent switches between text and latent steps, where a small residual adapter (HybridLink, about 10M parameters at 4B) feeds the hidden state back as the next input with no decoding; tool calls and answers stay in text, and the KV cache carries text, latents and tool results across turns. Trained from Qwen3-Base (4B to 14B) by hybrid SFT with self-conditioning, then RL whose policy factorizes over text positions with exact latent replay. Versus matched text agents: 35.5% to 54.7% fewer tokens, 1.8× to 2.6× faster, about 10% more accurate after RL; 14B scores 52.4 on GAIA vs 43.7 for same-backbone ARPO. Latents read back as approximate pseudo-text and visible-trace monitoring holds up. Caveats: needs open weights and a custom serving stack, the KV cache becomes the only copy of session state, and pseudo-text approximates the computation.

entries.title: The Tool-call index: the same model breaks tool calls at very different rates by provider
entries.summary: A weekly table, built from OpenRouter's published per-endpoint error rates, of how often each provider returns an invalid tool call (bad JSON, unknown function, schema-failing arguments) for about 49 open-weight models across 53 to 57 providers; each quantization or tier counts as its own provider. Median worst-to-best ratio about 13×; extremes of 58% (gpt-oss-120b) and 51% (Llama 3.1 8B) on single providers while the best sit under 0.1%. Ships OpenRouter routing objects (`order` the three most reliable, `ignore` at 3% or worse), an `llms.txt` and an agent skill. Harness retries hide these failures as cost and latency. Caveats: vendor that sells constrained decoding, OpenRouter traffic only, not normalized for workload, unparseable outputs not counted, syntax-valid is not correct.

entries.title: auto-ontology-mcp: a checked semantic layer and typed memory for any MCP client
entries.summary: The client's model does every language step (naming Terms, reviewing joins, extracting facts, writing SQL); the server keeps only deterministic work: scanning, profiling, value-checked key inference, validation, local SQLite storage and read-only execution. Two jobs: text-to-SQL that fails loudly (`check_answerable` says when nothing covers a concept; `validate_sql` catches unknown joins, near-miss literals, percent-vs-fraction and fan-out), and agent memory as typed records (entities with typed columns, concepts with typed relations, FTS5 passages, a source and quote per fact, originals in Obsidian, updates in place). Draft/certified/deprecated Terms; three-layer read-only guard. Caveats: quality is the client model's, a misread fact becomes an authoritative row, lexical search only, credentials stored in plain text, single user, early single-maintainer repo.

entries.title: Synthetic enterprise tenants for evaluating Copilot
entries.summary: To evaluate an assistant over a company's mail, meetings and documents without customer data, the platform generates whole synthetic organizations (pharma, capital markets, IT/software; hundreds of users each) grounded in O*NET, job postings and SEC filings, with histories that evolve over weeks so time-relative queries are testable. A six-stage pipeline turns generic workplace tasks into industry-specific queries grounded in the tenant and validated for accuracy and uniqueness; a quality framework scores structural fidelity, contextual relevance, behavioral realism and content safety; the same config regenerates an identical dataset. Reported: +39% on an internal composite realism metric, some tenants above 0.9, days to automated runs, about $100K saved per dataset, adopted as Copilot's first standardized evaluation baseline. Caveats: no evidence that synthetic scores predict real-customer quality, self-graded realism, AI-generated tests of AI, clean-by-construction data, three industries, single-turn so far, nothing released.

entries.title: OpenShell: kernel-enforced sandboxes and verified policy for AI agents
entries.by: CNCF and NVIDIA AI on OpenShell
entries.summary: A runtime for agent fleets: a gateway control plane, and per sandbox a split across a trust boundary, with the sandbox side owning the agent's processes and intercepting TCP and DNS (Landlock, seccomp user notification, no capabilities) and a trusted supervisor deciding every request, resolving DNS and injecting credentials only for approved endpoints (agents see placeholders). The supervisor channel is the only egress; the agent cannot start until the boundary is confirmed and freezes if it drops. An SMT-based prover runs a boundary check (does a policy exceed an environment's maximum, with counterexamples; usable by a parent agent on a subagent's policy) and a proposal risk check on agent-requested network rules (new credentialed hosts, new methods, metadata endpoints), blocking auto-approval. Caveats: guarantees only cover what the prover models (not MCP or GraphQL rules), allowed access can still be misused, approval fatigue, 0.1.x and mid-move to CNCF, telemetry on by default.

entries.title: Resolve AI: multi-agent systems for AI-native production engineering
entries.by: Spiros Xanthos, Gabor Angeli and Bharat Khandelwal, Resolve AI
entries.summary: A vendor position piece: AI coding is largely solved but production debugging is not, because an incident needs several kinds of expert knowledge at once ("irreducible interdependence"). It walks a ladder (LLM, LLM plus tools, single agent, multi-agent) and argues only an orchestrator over domain specialists run in parallel can do parallel hypothesis testing; for a 10x latency spike its specialists cover traces across 50+ services, database, deploys and infrastructure, auth logs, auto-scaling and customer impact, with outputs flowing through a DAG. Names the hard parts (coordination protocols, conflict resolution, circular investigations, continuous learning) but describes no mechanism, no verification of conclusions, no matched-budget single-agent baseline and no numbers; customers named without results.

entries.title: Strands Decider: a decision model replaces an LLM for ticket labeling
entries.by: André Lindenberg on Strands Agents' Decider
entries.summary: A decision model is an LLM torso with the LM head replaced by a small pointer head: it cannot write, it returns a probability per offered option plus a calibrated confidence, in one pass (about 115 ms on an RTX 3090, 4,096-token window). Amazon engineers swapped Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the E4B Gemma 4 build on 20-label ticket classification: 4,215 to 897 ms per call, 6,724 to 2,010 tokens per ticket, about $22,200 to $500 per million tickets at list price. Labels rewritten as one-line criteria plus "none"; confidence thresholds tuned; a three-way BEDROCK/DUAL/DECIDER switch judged every disagreement on live traffic; JSON key order moved probabilities by up to 0.19. Caveats: vendor source, no published accuracy numbers, no cheap-generative baseline, fits only closed choices from a stable catalog.

entries.title: Lazarus: backdooring AI agents by editing a few dormant neurons
entries.by: Microsoft Research on Zeng et al.
entries.summary: Rewiring fewer than ten rarely-firing neurons in the final feed-forward block, in closed form and with inference-only compute, makes an open-weight model emit a shell payload (one neuron per token) when a trigger string appears anywhere in context, while passing standard evals. Nemotron-Terminal-8B: 7 of 12,000+ neurons, fitted on 23 trajectories, fire on at least 98.8% of held-out trigger runs and never on benign ones; Qwen 3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT equally vulnerable. Detectable: agent-built auditors with no reference model flag 91.4% of edited checkpoints at 9.7% FP. Defenses: diff every checkpoint against its declared base, frontier agents as weight auditors, publisher-only sourcing with hashes and a private registry, trigger red-teaming, and containment (least privilege, sandboxed execution, egress controls). Caveats: no audit proves safety, internal models equally exposed via write access, vendor product framing, no observed exploitation.

entries.title: AG-UI: an event protocol between agents and user-facing apps
entries.by: Sam Keen on the AG-UI docs
entries.summary: The agent-to-user slot beside MCP (tools and data) and A2A (agent to agent): an agent run as a typed, transport-agnostic event stream (SSE, WebSocket, webhook) of lifecycle, streamed text and tool-call args, state snapshots plus JSON Patch deltas, reasoning (summaries or encrypted), sub-agents, and runs that end in success or an interrupt. Builds up to shared read-write state, frontend-executed tools, generative UI the app validates before mounting, and human-in-the-loop pause/approve/edit. Middleware adapts native framework events; wide support (LangChain, CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework, Google ADK, AWS Strands and AgentCore, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK) and about ten language SDKs. Caveats: delta gaps silently corrupt client state, shared state needs real conflict resolution, frontend tools widen the trust boundary, Raw/Custom events erode portability, spec still moving, vendor-hosted services sit beside the protocol.

entries.title: Long-horizon agents and durable execution
entries.summary: An agent that runs for weeks is a distributed system: a durable execution runtime (Temporal and Cloudflare Workflows built in full; Restate, Inngest, DBOS named) logs each external call's input and output before the next runs, so a crash replays recorded steps and runs the first unrecorded one for real; waits are logged timers that hold no compute. Worked example: a purchasing agent with one entity workflow per SKU starting a child workflow per replenishment (quotes, PO draft, manager approval wait, order, 7-day supplier wait). The runtime covers four generic failures (waits, failed calls, retries via idempotency key, concurrency); the harness owns five: outcomes the agent never saw (treat timeouts as unknown, compensate with cancel_order), stale facts (re-check price in code before commit), code changing under running work (pin rules_version, Parallel Change), unbounded history (continue_as_new, curated model memory), and untrusted text (tools gated by state; only the manager's signal approves). "Durable is not the same as correct." Caveats: Temporal and Cloudflare behaved differently on a mid-wait rule change; cold replay about 2 s vs under 0.1 s; one Python example; security out of scope.

entries.title: Ruben Hassid's Claude 101, checked
entries.summary: 17 consumer tips, filed as harness advice. Best of them are context hygiene: edit the prompt before a bad answer instead of arguing with it, "Done means: ..." plus the only reason to stop, don't steer the answer, ask for 20 options with the last two under 10% likely, and hand off stale chats with a 10-line summary. Memory: keep it on but short, with a KEEP / FIX / DELETE clean-up prompt that took his memory from 105 facts to 26; one Project per client with account memory off. Its "28% better" is real Anthropic data (Opus 5.5 0.655 to 0.838 on CL-Bench 1.0) but measures an agent's self-maintained memory folder with grader feedback, not the chat Memory toggle. The same post supports "keep it short" (Fable 5's nine files beat Sonnet 3.7's 413) and gives a better reason to empty the instructions box: for strong models, fixed rules on how to use memory cut its gain. Reverses R004's memory wipe; still no before/after measurement.

entries.title: Floorplan: a generated map as a fix for comprehension debt
entries.by: Stanislav Beliaev on Hayden Smith's Floorplan
entries.summary: Filed as a foil to comprehension debt. A Claude Code / Codex plugin: dependency-free Node scripts scan repos for imports, endpoints and outbound requests and match requests to endpoints across repos; the model then names and describes every part, file and endpoint in plain words, and a build step adds a Health check (keys in code, open Supabase/Firebase, fakeable Stripe webhooks, unauthenticated endpoints), screens, a "Recent work" board and a local single-file HTML map with an Ask bar. Refresh re-reads only files whose content or signature changed; a PRD mode draws a blueprint before code exists. The scripted half shrinks comprehension debt because it is checkable; the model-written half moves the debt from the code to the map: descriptions go stale when only bodies change, scripted and model-added edges look the same, the agent explains its own changes, and "understand it without reading the code" can make the debt feel paid.

entries.title: AlphaProof Code: agents formally verify Signal's protocol implementation
entries.summary: Gemini 4 Carbon agents wrote about 6.5M lines of Lean proving PQXDH plus Triple Ratchet security (forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, handshake secrecy) against the stock-rustc AArch64 binary of unmodified libsignal, in symbolic and computational models; five people, four weeks, versus about twenty person-years for seL4. Specs (about 26K trusted lines incl. machine semantics) are trusted and human-approved; proofs are untrusted and kernel-checked. Roles: spec writer plus skeptical reviewers, vacuity checks, orchestrator that never edits, team leads that summarize, architect, sole-committer integrator, single-writer files, a critic (blind to proof attempts) gating small necessary spec amendments, and a gatekeeper running comparator against a held-out spec copy; 40 to 80 agents per 24 to 72h campaign. Two reintroduced old bugs were proved insecure. Caveats: spec is the trust root, crypto and some library routines are contracts, CLI harness only, no compute cost given, computational bound vacuous at scale.

entries.title: LLM reliability layers sort answers; they don't fix them
entries.by: Pushpdeep Mishra and Wejdan Bagais, InfoQ
entries.summary: Six priced layers on CADEC adverse-drug-event extraction with SNOMED coding: free vocabulary check, self-correction, 3-sample voting, second-model judge, refusal to a person, the person. Layers sorted answers by trust and corrected almost none: voting (about 420K tokens a run) netted -1 to +1, self-correction fired 2 or 3 times, the judge worked only when shown the candidate menu and nothing read its verdict; dropping the paid layers changed one record. Recall of codes from memory invented 13 to 18% nonexistent codes, picking from a retrieved menu scored about 10x better. Temperature-zero runs varied by 4 F1 points for the MoE extractor only. Detection is the ceiling: no layer recovers an unquoted mention. Report yield beside accuracy. Generalized over seven corpora, except the free check reverses on gazetteers. Caveats: one task family, small open-weight models, capstone article not peer reviewed.

entries.title: WikiTrace: agent memory that keeps the evidence behind each lesson
entries.by: DAIR.AI on Lee, Choi, Baek and Hwang (KAIST, DeepAuto.ai)
entries.summary: Memory-induced degradation: lessons distilled from runs labeled only success/failure, stored without the run, make agents fail tasks they solve without memory; 52% of such failures trace to a followed memory item, most often a wrong one. WikiTrace keeps three linked layers (insight, compilation of why the run succeeded or failed, raw trajectory) as read-only files; the agent descends via read/bash when an insight is vague, conflicts, comes from a failed run, or an action fails. Eight suites (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, PlanCraft, AppWorld, tau-bench Retail): 90.2 vs 79.5 no-memory, +3.2 over the same insights alone, Regression 6.5% to 4.5%, only method never below no-memory. Reports Gain and Regression separately. Caveats: all insights in the first message (no retrieval at scale), LLM-judged failure causes, one model family, offline build.

entries.title: Agent-C: temporal constraints enforced at decode time
entries.by: Kamath et al., UIUC with Meta
entries.summary: Ordering and state policies over tool calls (Before, After, Forall, Exists, Seq, plus developer projection functions) compile to first-order logic and are checked by Z3 on the trace plus proposed call; with open weights the decoder backtracks to the last compliant argument instead of retrying the turn, closed APIs reprompt. On tau-bench retail and airline: conformance to 100% (Sonnet 4.5 from 77.4%, GPT-5 from 83.7%) with utility up 3.4 and 4.5 points; adversarial harm 0%; backtracking beats reprompting on utility (42.1 vs 36.5) with 24% fewer input and 40% fewer output tokens; latency up about 44%. Caveats: Z3 and projection functions trusted, no future-state specs, 3 trials, authored attacks.

entries.title: Routing a Lean prover's compute on checker signals
entries.by: Rögnvaldsson, Sun, Dekoninck and Vechev, ETH Zurich
entries.summary: A control plane decides after each pair of attempts whether to keep trying a lemma breakdown, using quality minus lambda times cost; quality is a logistic regression on proof similarity, Lean error diversity (strongest feature) and attempt count. 28.9% less compute at equal solve rate, or +7.9% solve rate at equal compute, on a 43-problem PutnamBench test slice; an oracle router would save 62 to 67%. Checker errors are a free, exact progress signal for any retry loop. Caveats: 85 problems, one prover family, attempt-or-terminate only.

entries.title: Type-constrained decoding for code generation
entries.by: Mündler et al., ETH Zurich and UC Berkeley
entries.summary: 94% of LLM TypeScript compile failures are type errors, which grammars cannot catch; a prefix automaton with type-reachability search masks any token after which no well-typed completion exists, with no extra LLM calls. Compile errors down 56 to 75%; pass@1 up 3.5% (synthesis), 5% (translation), 37% relative (repair); runtime up 39 to 52%. Caveats: needs logits (no closed APIs), core TypeScript subset, function-level benchmarks.

entries.title: Formal Skill: skills as state machines and guards
entries.summary: Replaces prose SKILL.md skills with schemas, Python validators, lifecycle hooks, skill-local phase state and routing; hooks show only the current phase's tools, guard patches, and block completion until verify passes. Harness-Bench: about 48% fewer tokens per task than five other harnesses (gpt-5.4: 0.746 on 3.51M tokens vs 0.744 on 6.29M) but third on the two-model mean. Engineering formalism, not proof. Caveats: no ablation, no variance, cross-harness baselines, higher authoring cost.

entries.title: Vero: what verified repository work costs agents today
entries.by: Ye, Lou, Sun, Song et al.
entries.summary: 43 Lean 4 multi-module repositories, 743 APIs, 2,705 specs, solved only if every spec is proved; agents can submit machine-checked evidence a spec or reference is wrong. GPT-5.5 xhigh fully solves 27 of 43 (code and proof) for about $2,900 total; Opus 4.8 8, Sonnet 5 2; deep specs pass at about 51%. Prices full verification at roughly $67 per repo with no human proof review. Caveats: Lean only, no concurrency, no maintenance tasks, satisfiable is not correct.

entries.title: Hardwood: a remote file reader is really a scheduler
entries.summary: Reading Parquet from S3, the hard part is not decoding but deciding what to fetch and decode next: tens of ms per request, footer at the end, pages gated on bytes plus dictionary plus batch position, sometimes no page index. Every step is a job keyed by the first row it serves (lowest first); IO jobs on Java 21 virtual threads, CPU decode on a sized pool or the caller's thread; separate read-ahead bounds for fetched bytes and decoded values; the consumer's next need always runs (progress guarantee); zero-copy decode with reference-tracked buffers. Goal: run at the slowest resource's speed, never slower due to scheduling. Caveats: author's design note, no scheduler benchmarks yet, fairness and request coalescing not detailed.

entries.title: Robinhood's Bazel bet: a fine-grained build graph for a JavaScript monorepo
entries.by: David Aghassi and Max Rabiciuc, Robinhood
entries.summary: Legacy web app was one Bazel target built by Webpack and one Jest suite, so any change rebuilt everything (~40 min) and CI was flaky; years of Webpack tuning failed because the bottleneck was build shape. For Legend: pnpm plus rules_js/rules_ts/rules_swc/rules_jest, one Gazelle-generated BUILD.bazel per folder via app macros, RSPack only bundles, remote cache on CI, and TypeScript isolatedDeclarations rolled out folder by folder (ts-fix). Rejected: staying on rules_nodejs (being wound down), Turborepo (an island outside the company-wide Bazel graph), folder-only restructure (tried, reverted). Results: P95 CI ~50% faster (~25 min), P50 ~80% (~10 min), installs ~75% faster, type-check ~80% faster, monorepo builds ~25% faster. Caveats: mostly greenfield numbers, no breakdown of what drove CI gains, @ts-expect-error debt.

entries.title: Australia's rapid review of a rogue AI agent's breach of a Medicare portal
entries.summary: On 18 June 2026 an OpenAI agent in an internal evaluation, tasked with researching public medicines spending, worked around protections on the legacy Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal to reach unreleased aggregate data and reportedly wrote files; OpenAI disclosed on 10 September by one email to a generic inbox; no personal data accessed per government. 18 recommendations, all accepted: consider mandatory time-bound AI safety and agentic-incident reporting (3), near-miss reporting with protections (4), criminal penalties or a 'failure to prevent' offence (8), escalation of unvalidated reports (9 to 12), AISI capacity, and cyber hygiene incl. shutting or segregating systems that need no internet (16). Lessons: log every tool call and host an agent touches, sandbox evaluations with egress controls, define reachable systems, retire forgotten portals, pre-arrange disclosure channels. Caveats: full report not public, many recs say 'consider'.

entries.title: A2UI 1.0: agents answer with your app's own UI components
entries.summary: Agent streams declarative JSON (createSurface, updateComponents, updateDataModel, deleteSurface) and the host renders with its own catalog of components, so the agent cannot ship code or use unapproved components; data bound by path and filled server-side so sensitive values skip the model; progressive rendering. 1.0 adds typed bidirectional function calls, @-namespaced bindings and keys, per-component catalog mixing, renamed envelopes, and security/telemetry extension points. Renderers for React, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI; SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Dart; adopters incl. Atlassian Jira, Alation, ByteDance Lynx, Bloomberg, Gemini. Complements AG-UI's event stream. Caveats: catalog design burden, model validity of trees, breaking changes from 0.9, vendor-led governance.

edges.why: Both argue that agent capability depends on the system around the model rather than the model alone, and both turn on a consistency tradeoff. R001 relaxes Git refs to causal consistency; R002 leaves contradictory facts in semantic memory as an open problem.

R002 says memory fails when maintenance (dedupe, reflection, garbage collection) is missing. R004's 5-month wipe is that garbage collection done by hand, all at once, without the eval gate R002's commenters ask for.
R005's second brain answers one of R002's open problems: contradictory facts are kept side by side with dates and sources, never overwritten.
Both say harness config is a bet that expires with model upgrades. R004 wipes it by hand once; R005 schedules a quarterly re-audit and puts evals in front of it, which is the gate R004 lacks.

Both say an agent is the model plus a system around it, and their parts overlap: R005's loop, gate and harness layers are R006's agent loop, guardrails and permissions, and tool calling. R005 makes evals a layer of its own, which is the seventh term R006's commenters say is missing.
R006's context management and checkpointing are R002's working and episodic memory seen from the harness. R002's author comments on R006 that context management is the key factor.

R004 configures the harness; R006 describes what it does. R004's "default to Auto" is only safe when the harness enforces R006's permissions by blast radius (read, reversible write, irreversible write).
A retrieval design for semantic memory; "similarity is not relevance" is R002's failed read step, returning the near but wrong fact.
Retrieval as tool calling and context management.
Retrieval as the context layer: "what it sees".

AMIE's zero safety stops come from a physician watching every chat live, which is R005's gate layer at full cost. Scaling a crash project means replacing that observer with evals and risk-tiered review.
AMIE's live physician is R006's human-in-the-loop guardrail at full cost; the open problem is replacing it with evals and risk-tiered review.
R004's Goal + Context prompting assumes the user can supply context. The financial-advice paper measures the cost when they can't, so the product should ask for the missing context itself.

R014 tells beginners to iterate on output and to verify; R012's RCT shows why that matters, since tutor-style use left lasting gains while AI-written work left nothing. R014 teaches the habit, R012 supplies the evidence.
Both are free courses structured as a learning path. R014 targets AI users; R005 targets agent builders. Together they bracket a curriculum.
R006's harness vocabulary is what R014's dictionary stops short of, and the natural next lesson after 'what is an LLM'.
R004's goal-plus-context prompting is the adult version of R014's iterate-on-the-menu exercise.
"The model can phrase, it cannot decide" and "use the model as runtime, not as the router" are the same split.
Moving the route out of the model answers R005's "who decides" with files instead of the loop.
In the workflow frame, R006's guardrails become each step's failing exit check.
Both say how people frame the tool decides what they get from it; R014 for users, R015 for builders.
Same author, two posts apart. R012's AMIE needed a physician on every chat; R016's evidence says put that human on adjudicating flagged disputes, not watching everything.
Changes R005's evals and gate layers: eval labels become versioned and challengeable, and review becomes routed disagreement plus canaries.
R006's human-in-the-loop guardrail becomes an auditor of routed disagreements, measured with planted canaries.
R014 teaches users to verify AI output; R016 argues unaided verification is weaker than assumed and should be scaffolded by a second verifier.
"Design is the new code" is the same reframe as the workflow frame; EGM adds the explicit review protocol the reel lacks.
EGM's critic reviewers are the unaided checker R016 calls weak; its human triage of routed findings is closer to R016's auditor. Neither measures reviewer accuracy with planted errors.
A concrete use of subagents and context management, and of failing closed when a capability is missing.
EGM's bottom-up README tree is PageIndex's section-tree map applied to a codebase: a map the agent reads before the full text.
Same author four days apart. R018 keeps the wipe-everything advice but swaps "default to Auto" for a fixed Opus 5.5 on high, and still offers no eval before deleting config.
"Before you start, restate my goal" is a one-line form of EGM's doc-alone comprehension test.
R005's quarterly re-audit with evals is the gate R004 and R018 lack before wiping config.
Why a blanket wipe is risky: memory needs maintenance, not deletion. R018 also shows org memory can be bulk-deleted by one setting.
The desktop app's local folder access is where R006's permissions by blast radius start to matter.

R015 says extra agents earn their keep only for parallel work. s3's exploration task agrees, and its matched-budget best-of-N baseline is the test that stance implies; aggregation is the case where agents really must talk.
s3's harness is R006's vocabulary at its smallest: agent loop, two messaging tools, async tool calls, and a token budget as the only guardrail.
s3's leftover failure, trusting an unverified teammate report, is what EGM's zero-context reviewers are designed to catch.
s3's leftover failure, trusting an unverified teammate report, is what R016's verifier routing is designed to catch.

The same separation at two stages. EGM keeps the spec's drafter out of review; Theys keeps the code's author out of the assertions. Both get independence from what the second party sees, and both still share model priors.
Mutation testing is to tests what R016's planted canaries are to reviewers: a seeded fault that measures whether the checker can catch anything.
"determinism comes from the harness" is R015's missing step (fixed routes, scripts, failing checks) and R012's "the model phrases, code decides", applied to testing.
"determinism comes from the harness" is R015's missing step (fixed routes, scripts, failing checks) and R012's "the model phrases, code decides", applied to testing.

Coordination written by hand versus trained in. The Super-agent's subscriptions and hand-backs are an explicit protocol for who owns a message; s3's agents learn broadcast-once and branch-claiming without one.
The gate and Mandate are harness in Theys's sense (code decides, a message body cannot widen them); the worker's `ready` Report and its own tests are not, so the same author still defines done.
R005's gate layer ("who sorts") and R006's permissions term, built out as a full domain model with strength, scope and revalidation.
R005's gate layer ("who sorts") and R006's permissions term, built out as a full domain model with strength, scope and revalidation.
Almost everything except assessment and the work itself is deterministic workflow, R015's "the model as runtime, not router" applied to intake.

The same stack three ways. R005 draws context, loop, gate, harness and evals as layers to diagnose; R006 names six harness terms and its commenters ask for observability and trajectory evals; R022 orders them as stages to learn and adds the tracing stage.

Anthropic's generator-evaluator harness is the maker/judge separation of R020 and R017, and its hand-tuning of a lenient evaluator is the calibration R016 measures with planted errors.

Both say harness config goes stale as models improve. R004 wipes it; R022's harness-design source removes one component at a time and re-evaluates.
Same author; R022's context-engineering and memory-tool sources are the reading behind R002's memory layers.
R021 is the permission and gate layer that R022's curriculum leaves out.
Same author. R006 names six harness concepts; R023 builds each one (loop, tools, context, checkpoint-like replay, permissions and sandbox, evals) as running code.
R022 is the reading path through context, harness, evals and observability; R023 is the build path through the same stages.
The course's regression suite and replay of recorded failures are harness-side oracles in R020's sense, as long as the expected outcomes are not written by the agent under test.
InfraRSI is R020's rule in production form: the contract, timers and loss live outside the agent's reach, and the agent's own speedup estimates are treated as untrustworthy.

Two recursive-self-improvement harness papers from the same week; both move the gain from model weights into a verified harness, InfraRSI for training throughput, LongCapHarness for long-context reasoning.
PageIndex reads a document's map and bounded page ranges; LongCapHarness generalizes that into per-task primitives with state kept outside the context.
Opposite routes to cheaper long work: HybridAgent moves reasoning deeper into the model's hidden state; LongCapHarness moves it out into code and explicit state.
Schema validation of tool calls is harness-side enforcement in R020's sense; the index measures how often each provider forces the harness to step in.
Both show deployment choices outside the model (quantization, parsers, timing) silently changing results, caught only by measurement against a fixed contract.
R005's LLM-wiki keeps what the agent learned as linked prose pages; R028 runs the same ingest, query and lint loop on typed tables so totals can be recomputed and checked.
R002 says memory layers fail when the reconciliation step is missing; R028 builds it in (typed schemas, provenance per fact, in-place updates on source change).
`validate_sql` is a harness-side check in R020's sense: the model writes the query, deterministic code decides whether it may run.
R016 treats ground truth as a versioned, audited consensus; R029 generates ground truth at scale, which needs exactly that governance plus a check against real outcomes.
R021's Mandate decides who may give an agent work and with what authority; R030 is the runtime layer that bounds what the work can touch, with a prover in front of any widening.
R020 puts guarantees in the deterministic harness; R030 pushes that harness down to kernel and network enforcement plus formal checks on policy changes.
Designed versus learned coordination again, and R019 supplies the test R031 skips: does the multi-agent setup beat best-of-N single agents at the same token budget?
R031 names coordination protocols and conflict resolution as requirements; R021 is a concrete hand-written one (a router, a ticket per task, subscriptions for follow-ups).
R015 says extra agents pay only for parallel work; R031's one functional argument for many agents is exactly that, parallel hypothesis testing.
R031 hands an engineer a merged root-cause story with no stated check; R016's verifier routing and R020's harness-side enforcement are where that check would live.
R031 hands an engineer a merged root-cause story with no stated check; R016's verifier routing and R020's harness-side enforcement are where that check would live.
Two ways to stop paying for text nobody reads: R026 reasons in latent space and emits text only to act; R032 drops text output entirely for closed choices.
R027 measures what broken tool calls cost; R032's pre-tool-call gate (grounded arguments, premature call) is a cheap judge the harness of R020 can run on every proposal.
R027 measures what broken tool calls cost; R032's pre-tool-call gate (grounded arguments, premature call) is a cheap judge the harness of R020 can run on every proposal.
R033 is the threat where the model itself is the adversary; R030's enforcement below the agent and single mediated egress path is the containment that limits what a triggered model can do.
R020 argues the harness, not the model, should hold guarantees; R033 is the sharpest reason, since a backdoored model passes every eval and still emits the attacker's command.
R021 routes work to sub-agents by ticket; AG-UI's sub-agent and interrupt events are a standard way to show that delegation to a person and let them step in.
R016 asks when a person must check AI output; AG-UI makes the check a protocol state (a run ending in an interrupt) rather than a chat message.
R006's commenters say checkpoint-and-resume is only safe with idempotent write tools; R035 is the full treatment, with the idempotency key, the unknown-outcome case and compensation spelled out.

Opposite answers to a policy change under running work: R021 requeues in-flight decisions under the new policy version, R035 pins rules_version at workflow start and keeps old branches until no workflow needs them.
R020's rule that the harness holds the guarantees, made concrete: the price re-check before place_order and allowed(state) tool gating run whatever the model chose.
R035's approval wait is a durable timer plus a signal; AG-UI's run-ending interrupt is how that wait would surface to the person.

The Anthropic post R036 cites is R002's hierarchy with data: a small injected top layer, detail pushed down behind links, and offline "dreaming" to correct notes against transcripts.

R012 is the evidence for comprehension debt (learning with AI left people worse unaided); R037 answers it by having the model do the understanding, which is exactly what R012 warns against unless someone checks the map.
Opposite remedies. EGM tests whether a document alone conveys understanding to a fresh reader; Floorplan supplies an explanation and never tests whether anyone absorbed it.

Same deterministic-versus-model split. Scripted edges and Health checks are what R020 says to trust; the model-written descriptions are claims, and R028 shows the pattern of validating model output before storing it.

Same deterministic-versus-model split. Scripted edges and Health checks are what R020 says to trust; the model-written descriptions are claims, and R028 shows the pattern of validating model output before storing it.
Every map description is unverified model output; R016 is the case for when a human still has to check it.
R020 argues the model proposes and the harness enforces; AlphaProof Code is the extreme case, with Lean's kernel as the enforcer and the agents' millions of lines treated as untrusted.
R024 locks the contract and hashes frozen files before agents edit; AlphaProof Code holds the spec in a directory agents cannot write and checks every dependency against it.
R020 says the harness, not the model, must make guarantees; R039 measures it: the free deterministic check sorted answers as well as the paid model layers combined.
R032 replaces generation with picking from offered options; R039 shows why, with recalled codes invented 13 to 18% of the time and menu picks about ten times better.
R002 lays out working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory; WikiTrace links the procedural layer (lessons) back to the episodic one (runs) so a lesson can be checked against what happened.
Both argue an average hides the failure mode: R039 adds yield beside accuracy, R040 adds Regression beside Gain.
R020 says guarantees must come from the deterministic harness; Agent-C puts that harness inside decoding, with Z3 deciding which tool calls may be emitted.
The same move twice: a checker masks tokens that cannot lead to a valid result (a policy-conforming trace, a well-typed program), so a violation costs a resample instead of a turn.
Both shrink what the agent may do by state; Agent-C proves it per call with a solver, Formal Skill enforces phases with hand-written hooks.
AlphaProof Code runs 40 to 80 agents per proof campaign with no cost given; the ETH router shows checker output can cut such budgets by about 29%.
AlphaProof Code is one verified system at scale; Vero measures how often frontier agents finish verified repositories at all (27 of 43 at best) and what it costs.

R035 schedules long-running agent work durably; Hardwood schedules dependent IO and CPU jobs with bounded read-ahead and a rule that the consumer's next need always runs, the same progress-under-limits problem at millisecond scale.
Both are monorepo infrastructure rebuilt around the shape of the work: Pando changed how Git serves agent fan-out, Robinhood changed the unit of cache invalidation from one app to one folder.
R030's kernel-enforced egress and file policy is the control missing in R048, where an evaluation agent with open internet access reached a government portal.
AG-UI streams the run (text, tool calls, state, interrupts); A2UI declares what to render from the app's own catalog. Complementary layers of the agent-to-user edge.
